sections.title: Start here
sections.body:
Statics is about things that are not moving. If a beam or a truss sits still, every push on it is cancelled by another push, and every twist by another twist.

Almost every question is the same three steps: draw the body on its own, mark every force, and write that forces and moments each add to zero.
pitfalls: Leaving a support reaction off the free body diagram.
Taking moments about a point that makes the arithmetic harder. Pick a point where an unknown force passes through.

tips.from: Mark Mattson, FE Statics Review Session 2022
items: Write your sign convention on the page before summing anything (for example up positive, counter-clockwise positive) and keep it for the whole problem.
Draw the free-body diagram every time, even when the problem looks short.
A mass is not a force. Multiply kilograms by 9.81 to get newtons, and watch N against kN.
Carry the digits. Do not round an intermediate value toward an answer choice that looks close.
Read the whole question first; what it asks for is often not the first thing you would solve for.
In the method of joints, draw each member force's x and y components separately so they are not mixed up.
For a composite moment of inertia, split the section into simple shapes and use the parallel axis theorem. Do not swap in an 'equivalent' rectangle, because the A d^{2} term dominates.
On an incline, line the axes up with the surface.
Know the common unit conversions by heart; looking them up costs time.

bridge.plain: Statics is the study of things that do not move. If an object stays still, every push on it is cancelled by another, and every turning effect is cancelled too. From that one fact you can find the unknown forces holding it up.
core: A force has a size and a direction; split it into a horizontal and a vertical part.
A moment is a force's turning effect: force times perpendicular distance.
Draw the object alone with every force on it (a free-body diagram), then write: sum of horizontal forces = 0, sum of vertical forces = 0, sum of moments = 0.
Shape properties, the centroid and the moment of inertia, are found by adding up simple pieces.
bridge.links: Everything structural starts here: mechanics of materials turns these forces into stresses, structural analysis applies them to beams and frames, geotechnics uses them for walls and slopes, and fluids uses them for water pressure on surfaces.
bridge.exam: Finding support reactions is the first step of a large share of exam questions, so it is the first skill to rebuild.

sections.title: Resultants of force systems
sections.body:
A resultant is the single force that has the same effect as several forces acting together. To find it, break every force into x and y parts, add the x parts, add the y parts, and recombine with the right-triangle rule.

A force also tends to turn a body about a point. That turning effect is its moment: the force times the perpendicular distance from the point to the force's line of action. Use a sign convention, such as counter-clockwise positive, and stick to it.

formulas.name: Components
formulas.expr: F_{x} = F cos(angle), F_{y} = F sin(angle)

pitfalls: Using the full length of a member as the moment arm when the force is not perpendicular to it.
Measuring the angle from the wrong axis.
Answering with one component when the question asks for the resultant, or the other way round.

ideas.title: Slope triangles instead of angles
ideas.text: When a direction is given as a slope, such as 3 vertical in 4 horizontal, the components are the force times the side ratios of that triangle: 3/5 and 4/5 of the force. No angle has to be found.

ideas.title: Resultant
ideas.text: Concurrent forces add as vectors. Resolve each force into x and y components, add the components, then recombine with the Pythagorean theorem. The resultant is always less than the arithmetic sum unless the forces are parallel.

ideas.title: Moments
ideas.text: Only the force component perpendicular to the lever arm produces moment: M = F L sin(angle between force and arm). The component along the arm passes through the pivot and contributes nothing.

ideas.title: Resolution of a force
ideas.text: When a direction is given as a slope, the components are the force times the side ratios of the slope triangle. The hypotenuse is the square root of rise squared plus run squared.

sections.deep:
A system of forces can be replaced by a single resultant that has the same effect. Because forces are vectors, the resultant comes from adding components, never magnitudes. Choose axes that make the components easy, usually horizontal and vertical.

In three dimensions the idea is identical with one more component. Direction cosines or a unit vector along the line of action give the components of a force whose line passes through two known points.
method: Draw the forces from a common point and choose x and y axes.
Resolve each force: F cos(angle) along the axis the angle is measured from, F sin(angle) along the other.
Add the x components and the y components, keeping signs.
Recombine: magnitude by the Pythagorean theorem, direction by the inverse tangent.
Check the quadrant of the angle against the signs of the components.
sections.credit: Some of the points in this lesson follow Mark Mattson's 2022 FE review session for this topic, restated in this site's words.
sections.primer: A force is a push or a pull with a size and a direction. Any force can be replaced by two parts at right angles: a horizontal component and a vertical component, found with sine and cosine. To combine several forces, add their horizontal parts, add their vertical parts, and the two totals give the single resultant force.
terms: resultant
the single force that has the same effect as several forces acting together
moment
the turning effect of a force about a point: the force times its perpendicular distance from that point
symbols: perpendicular distance (moment arm), or distance between parallel axes

sections.title: Equivalent force systems
sections.body:
Two force systems are equivalent if they push and turn a body in exactly the same way. Any set of forces can be replaced by one force at a chosen point plus one couple.

A couple is a pair of equal, opposite, parallel forces. It produces pure turning with no net push, and its moment is the same about every point. When you move a force to a new point, keep the force unchanged and add a couple equal to the moment the original force had about the new point.

formulas.name: Couple
formulas.expr: M = F × d (d is the distance between the forces)

pitfalls: Changing the size or direction of the force when moving it. Only a couple is added.
Placing the resultant of a triangular load at mid-length.

example.problem: A 400 N force acts at the end of a 0.5 m bracket. Replace it with a force and couple at the wall.
example.steps:
The force at the wall is still 400 N.

The couple is 400(0.5) = 200 N·m.

ideas.title: Distributed loads as single forces
ideas.text: A uniform load w over a length L acts as w L at mid-length. A triangular load acts as half its peak intensity times its length, one third of the length from the tall end. Split a trapezoidal load into a rectangle and a triangle.

ideas.title: Locating the equivalent force
ideas.text: The single force that replaces a set of loads sits where it gives the same moment: distance = sum of moments / sum of forces. A centroid is the same calculation with areas in place of forces.

ideas.title: Couple
ideas.text: A couple is two equal, opposite, parallel forces. Its moment is force × perpendicular distance between the lines of action, and it is the same about every point, so a couple is a free vector.

ideas.title: Couple
ideas.text: A force can be moved to a parallel line of action if a couple is added equal to the moment of the original force about the new point. The force keeps its magnitude and direction; the couple is M = F d.

examples.problem: Three parallel downward forces act on a beam: 22 kN at the left end, 12 kN at 2.2 m and 18 kN at 6 m from the left end. How far from the left end does their single resultant act?
examples.idea: A single force replaces a set of parallel forces if it has the same total and the same moment about any point. Its position is the sum of the moments divided by the sum of the forces.
examples.steps:
Sum of forces = 22 + 12 + 18 = 52 kN.

Sum of moments about the left end = 12(2.2) + 18(6) = 134.4 kN·m.

Position = \frac{134.4}{52} = 2.58 m.

sections.deep:
Two force systems are equivalent if they have the same resultant force and the same resultant moment about any point. That lets you move a force to a more convenient point, provided you add a couple equal to the moment the force had about that point.

A couple is pure turning effect with no net force, and its moment is the same about every point. Reducing a loading to one force and one couple at a chosen point is the first step in analysing supports, bolt groups and footings.
method: Pick the point where the equivalent system is wanted.
Sum the forces; that resultant acts at the chosen point.
Sum the moments of all forces and couples about that point; that is the accompanying couple.
To find a single equivalent force with no couple, place the resultant at a distance equal to the moment divided by the force.

sections.primer: A force also tries to turn an object. That turning effect is its moment: the force times the perpendicular distance from the force's line to the point of interest. Any set of forces can be replaced by one force plus one moment that have the same overall effect.
sections.work: A signal mast arm carries its signal heads at a distance from the pole, so the pole base feels both their weight and a moment.
terms: moment
the turning effect of a force about a point: the force times its perpendicular distance from that point
couple
two equal and opposite forces a distance apart; together they only turn an object and do not push it anywhere
resultant
the single force that has the same effect as several forces acting together
centroid
the geometric centre of an area, the point where it would balance if cut from uniform card
symbols: perpendicular distance between the two forces
distance from the reference axis to a centroid

sections.title: Equilibrium of rigid bodies
sections.body:
A body at rest is in equilibrium: the forces on it cancel and the moments on it cancel. In a plane that gives three equations, so you can solve for three unknowns.

The method never changes. Draw the free body diagram: the body alone, with every load and every support reaction shown. A pin gives two reaction components, a roller gives one perpendicular to its surface, and a fixed support gives two forces and a moment. Then take moments about a point where unknowns pass through, so they drop out of the equation.

formulas.name: Equilibrium in a plane
formulas.expr: sum F_{x} = 0, sum F_{y} = 0, sum M = 0

pitfalls: Leaving a reaction off the free body diagram.
Replacing a distributed load with a point load at the wrong place. It acts at the centroid of the load diagram.
Sign slips when moving moment terms across the equals sign. Re-check the sense of each term.
Using a mass in kilograms as a force. Multiply by 9.81 for newtons and divide by 1,000 for kilonewtons.

example.problem: A 9 m beam on a pin at A and a roller at B carries 18 kN at 3 m from A. Find the reactions.
example.steps:
Moments about A: B(9) = 18(3), so B = 6 kN.

A = 18 - 6 = 12 kN.

ideas.title: Where to take moments
ideas.text: Take moments about the point that the most unknown forces pass through. Each of them drops out, and one equation often gives the answer directly.

ideas.title: Equilibrium requirements
ideas.text: A beam in equilibrium satisfies two conditions: the moments about any point sum to zero and the vertical forces sum to zero. Taking moments about A removes A_{y} from the equation and gives B_{y} directly. The support nearer the load carries the larger share.

ideas.title: Equilibrium requirements
ideas.text: Replace the uniform load by its resultant, w L, acting at midspan. With every load centred, the loading is symmetric and each support carries half of the total.

ideas.title: Concurrent forces
ideas.text: At the joint the vertical components of the two cable tensions must carry the weight: 2 T sin(angle) = W. The flatter the cables, the larger the tension, and it grows without limit as the angle approaches zero.

ideas.title: Equilibrium requirements
ideas.text: A triangular load acts as a single force equal to half its peak intensity times its length, placed one third of the length from the tall end. With the resultant known, take moments about A.

examples.problem: A simply supported beam spans 12 m between a pin at A and a roller at B. A single 48 kN load acts 3 m from A. What is the vertical reaction at A?
examples.idea: A beam in equilibrium satisfies two conditions: the moments about any point sum to zero and the vertical forces sum to zero. Taking moments about A removes A_{y} from the equation and gives B_{y} directly. The support nearer the load carries the larger share.
examples.steps:
Moments about A: B_{y}(12) = 48(3), so B_{y} = 12 kN.

Vertical forces: A_{y} = 48 - 12 = 36 kN.

Check with the lever rule: A_{y} = 48 × (12 - 3) / 12 = 36 kN.

examples.problem: A 1,500 N weight hangs from two cables. Each cable makes an angle of 45° with the horizontal. What is the tension in each cable?
examples.idea: At the joint the vertical components of the two cable tensions must carry the weight: 2 T sin(angle) = W. The flatter the cables, the larger the tension, and it grows without limit as the angle approaches zero.
examples.steps:
Vertical forces at the joint: 2 T sin 45° = 1,500.

T = \frac{1,500}{2 sin 45°} = \frac{1,500}{1.414} = 1,061 N.

sections.deep:
A rigid body at rest must satisfy equilibrium: the forces sum to zero and the moments about any point sum to zero. In a plane that is three independent equations, so three unknown reactions can be found.

The free-body diagram is the whole method. Isolate the body, replace each support by the reactions it can supply (a roller one force, a pin two, a fixed support two forces and a moment) and show every load. Taking moments about a point where two unknowns meet leaves one equation with one unknown.
method: Draw the free-body diagram with every load and reaction.
Replace distributed loads by their resultants at their centroids.
Take moments about a support to eliminate its reactions and solve for the other.
Sum vertical and horizontal forces for the rest.
Check by taking moments about a different point.

sections.primer: An object at rest is in equilibrium: the forces on it add to zero in every direction, and so do their moments. Draw the object by itself with every load and every support force (a free-body diagram), write those balance equations, and solve them for the unknown support forces, called reactions.

terms: equilibrium
the state of an object that is not accelerating: all forces on it cancel, and so do all their turning effects
moment
the turning effect of a force about a point: the force times its perpendicular distance from that point
free-body diagram
a sketch of one object on its own with every force acting on it drawn as an arrow; the first step of almost every force problem
reaction
the force a support pushes back with to hold a structure in place
resultant
the single force that has the same effect as several forces acting together

sections.title: Frames and trusses
sections.body:
A truss is built from straight members pinned at their ends and loaded only at the joints. Each member carries only tension or compression along its length.

Two methods solve a truss. The method of joints isolates one pin and balances forces in x and y: use it when you need many member forces. The method of sections cuts through the truss and balances one whole piece: use it when you need one or two members. Zero-force members can be spotted by inspection: at an unloaded joint where two members meet at an angle, both carry zero. Frames have members that carry bending, so take them apart and write equilibrium for each piece.
pitfalls: Assuming the wrong sense and not correcting the sign: a negative answer means the opposite of what you assumed.
Cutting more than three unknown members in a section.
Forgetting that a diagonal member carries horizontal force at a joint as well as vertical.

example.problem: A symmetric triangular truss spans 6 m and is 4 m high with 30 kN at the apex. Find the force in an inclined member.
example.steps:
Each reaction is 15 kN. The inclined member is 5 m long, so sin(angle) = \frac{4}{5}.

F = \frac{15}{0.8} = 18.75 kN compression.

ideas.title: Force triangles match geometry triangles
ideas.text: A cable or truss member carries force only along its own line, so the components of its force are in the same ratio as the member's rise, run and length. Use those ratios instead of solving for the angle.

ideas.title: Assume tension
ideas.text: Draw every unknown member force pulling away from the joint. A positive answer is then tension and a negative one compression, with no guessing.

ideas.title: Method of joints
ideas.text: Use the method of joints at a support. Only the inclined member has a vertical component there, so its vertical component must equal the support reaction. The member force is the reaction divided by the sine of the member's angle.

ideas.title: Method of joints
ideas.text: At a support joint the horizontal component of the inclined member must be balanced by the bottom member. The inclined member is in compression, so the bottom chord is in tension and acts as a tie.

examples.problem: A symmetric triangular truss spans 16 m and is 6 m high. A 60 kN load acts at the apex. What is the force in each inclined member?
examples.idea: Use the method of joints at a support. Only the inclined member has a vertical component there, so its vertical component must equal the support reaction. The member force is the reaction divided by the sine of the member's angle.
examples.steps:
By symmetry each reaction is 60 / 2 = 30 kN.

Inclined member length = \sqrt{8^{2} + 6^{2}} = 10 m, so sin(angle) = 6 / 10.

Joint at the support, vertical forces: F × \frac{6}{10} = 30, so F = 50 kN (compression).

sections.deep:
A truss is built from two-force members pinned at joints and loaded only at joints, so each member carries pure tension or compression. The method of joints applies force equilibrium at one pin at a time. The method of sections cuts the truss in two and applies all three equilibrium equations to one piece, which reaches an interior member directly.

Frames and machines contain multi-force members, so they are taken apart member by member with equal and opposite forces at the connecting pins. Spot zero-force members first: at an unloaded joint with two non-collinear members, both carry zero.
method: Find the support reactions from the whole truss.
For a member near a support, use the method of joints, starting at a joint with at most two unknowns.
For an interior member, cut through at most three members and take moments about the point where two of them meet.
Assume unknown forces are tension; a negative answer means compression.
Check with the remaining equilibrium equation.
sections.credit: Some of the points in this lesson follow Mark Mattson's 2022 FE review session for this topic, restated in this site's words.
sections.primer: A truss is a frame of straight bars joined at their ends, loaded only at the joints, so each bar is purely pulled (tension) or pushed (compression). Find a bar's force by isolating one joint, or by cutting through the truss and balancing one side.

the state of an object that is not accelerating: all forces on it cancel, and so do all their turning effects
reaction

sections.title: Centroid of area
sections.body:
The centroid is the balance point of a shape: the spot where a cardboard cutout would balance on a pin. For a symmetric shape it lies on the axis of symmetry.

For built-up shapes, split the area into simple pieces, find each piece's area and centroid, and take the area-weighted average. A hole is handled as a piece with negative area. The handbook tabulates centroids of common shapes.
pitfalls: Measuring the piece centroids from different reference lines.

sections.deep:
The centroid is the geometric centre of an area, the point where it would balance if cut from uniform sheet. For a composite shape it is the area-weighted average of the centroids of the simple parts, and holes count as negative areas.

Any axis of symmetry passes through the centroid, which often gives one coordinate for free. The handbook tabulates centroids of common shapes: a triangle's is one third of the height from the base, a semicircle's is 4r / (3 pi) from the diameter.
method: Choose a reference axis, usually the bottom or left edge.
Split the shape into rectangles, triangles and circles; treat cut-outs as negative.
Tabulate each part's area and the distance from the axis to its own centroid.
Divide the sum of area times distance by the sum of areas.
Check that the answer lies inside the shape's extent and on any axis of symmetry.
sections.primer: The centroid of a shape is its balance point. For a shape made of simple pieces, multiply each piece's area by the distance to its own centre, add those up, and divide by the total area.

the geometric centre of an area, the point where it would balance if cut from uniform card

sections.title: Area moments of inertia
sections.body:
The area moment of inertia measures how a shape's area is spread out from an axis. The farther the material sits from the axis, the stiffer the shape is in bending about it. That is why beams are deep rather than wide.

Use tabulated formulas for simple shapes about their own centroid, then shift to another axis with the parallel axis theorem. For built-up shapes, shift each piece to the common axis and add. The radius of gyration turns I into an equivalent distance and appears in column design.
pitfalls: Cubing the wrong dimension: the dimension perpendicular to the axis is the one cubed.
Applying the parallel axis theorem from an axis that is not the centroidal one.

example.problem: Find I about the centroidal axis for a rectangle 50 mm wide and 120 mm deep.

figure.caption: The centroidal axis of a rectangle. I about this axis is b h^{3} / 12.

ideas.title: Parts that share the axis add directly
ideas.text: When the parts of a section have their centroids on the axis in question, their moments of inertia add or subtract with no parallel-axis term; a channel about its mid-height is a large rectangle minus a smaller one. The A d^{2} term appears only for parts offset from the axis, and it often dominates.

ideas.title: Moment of inertia
ideas.text: For a rectangle about its own centroidal axis, I = b h^{3} / 12, where h is the dimension perpendicular to the axis. Depth is cubed, so doubling the depth gives eight times the stiffness.

ideas.title: Parallel axis
ideas.text: The parallel axis theorem moves a moment of inertia from the centroidal axis to a parallel axis: I = I_{c} + A d^{2}. For a rectangle about its base, d = h/2, which gives I = b h^{3} / 3, four times the centroidal value.

examples.idea: The parallel axis theorem moves a moment of inertia from the centroidal axis to a parallel axis: I = I_{c} + A d^{2}. For a rectangle about its base, d = h/2, which gives I = b h^{3} / 3, four times the centroidal value.

examples.idea: When shapes share the same centroidal axis their moments of inertia add or subtract directly. Take the outer rectangle's b h^{3} / 12 and subtract the opening's.

examples.problem: A symmetric I-section has flanges 150 mm wide and 18 mm thick, and a web 10 mm thick and 263 mm high between them. What is its moment of inertia about the horizontal centroidal axis?
examples.idea: The web sits on the centroidal axis, so only its own b h^{3} / 12 counts. Each flange is offset, so the parallel axis theorem adds its area times the square of the distance from the axis to the flange's centroid. That term usually dominates.

examples.idea: The radius of gyration is the square root of the moment of inertia divided by the area. For a rectangle about its centroidal axis this is h divided by the square root of 12.

examples.idea: The polar moment of inertia of a circle is π d^{4} / 32, twice the moment of inertia about a diameter. For a tube, subtract the bore.

sections.deep:
The area moment of inertia measures how far an area is spread from an axis, weighting distance squared. It governs bending stiffness and bending stress, which is why depth matters so much more than width.

The parallel axis theorem moves it between parallel axes: I = I about the centroid + A d^{2}. It only works starting from the centroidal axis. For a composite section, find the centroid first, then add each part's own I plus its A d^{2}. The radius of gyration is the square root of I / A.
method: Locate the centroid of the whole section.
For each part, write its own centroidal I from the handbook table.
Add A d^{2} for each part, with d measured from the part's centroid to the section's centroid.
Sum the contributions; subtract those of holes.
Check units of length to the fourth power.

sections.primer: The moment of inertia of an area measures how far its material lies from an axis. Material far from the axis counts much more, by distance squared. It decides how stiff and strong a beam's cross-section is in bending. For built-up shapes, add the pieces, shifting each to the common axis.

terms: moment
the turning effect of a force about a point: the force times its perpendicular distance from that point
moment of inertia
a measure of how far an area's material is spread from an axis; the larger it is, the stiffer the shape in bending about that axis
centroid
the geometric centre of an area, the point where it would balance if cut from uniform card
parallel axis theorem
the rule for moving a moment of inertia to a parallel axis: add the area times the square of the distance between the axes
radius of gyration
the distance from an axis at which the whole area (or mass) could be concentrated and keep the same moment of inertia
symbols: moment of inertia about the centroidal axis
moment of inertia about the base
moment of inertia of the area

sections.title: Static friction
sections.body:
Friction is the grip between two surfaces. It resists sliding and adjusts itself to match whatever force is trying to cause motion, up to a limit. That limit is the coefficient of static friction times the force pressing the surfaces together.

If the applied force is less than the limit, nothing moves and friction simply equals the applied force. At the limit, motion is about to start. On a slope, sliding starts when the tangent of the slope angle equals the friction coefficient.

formulas.name: Belt friction
formulas.expr: T_{1} = T_{2}e^{μ × wrap angle in radians}

pitfalls: Assuming friction always equals μN. That is only its maximum.
Using the weight as the normal force on a slope or when a force has a vertical part.

example.problem: A 300 N box rests on a floor with a friction coefficient of 0.4. A 90 N horizontal push is applied. Does it move, and what is the friction force?
example.steps:
Maximum friction = 0.4(300) = 120 N.

The 90 N push is below the limit, so the box stays put and friction is 90 N.

ideas.title: Each sliding surface has its own normal force
ideas.text: With stacked blocks, friction acts on every face that slides. The upper face carries the weight above it; the lower face carries both blocks. Find each normal force separately.

ideas.title: A horizontal push on an incline
ideas.text: A horizontal force on a block on a slope has a component into the surface, so it raises the normal force and with it the friction. Put the axes along and across the slope and solve the two equilibrium equations together.

ideas.title: Friction
ideas.text: On an incline the weight component along the slope is W sin(angle) and the largest friction force available is (coefficient) × W cos(angle). Sliding is about to start when these are equal, which gives tan(angle) = coefficient of static friction. The weight cancels, so the angle does not depend on it.

ideas.title: Friction
ideas.text: The upward component of the rope force reduces the normal force, which reduces the friction available. Write equilibrium in both directions at impending motion: horizontal pull = coefficient × (weight minus vertical pull).

ideas.title: Friction
ideas.text: Each sliding surface has its own normal force. The top face of the lower block carries the upper block's weight; its bottom face carries both. Friction on both faces opposes the pull.

examples.problem: A crate rests on a ramp. The coefficient of static friction between the crate and the ramp is 0.45. What is the steepest ramp angle at which the crate stays put?
examples.idea: On an incline the weight component along the slope is W sin(angle) and the largest friction force available is (coefficient) × W cos(angle). Sliding is about to start when these are equal, which gives tan(angle) = coefficient of static friction. The weight cancels, so the angle does not depend on it.
examples.steps:
At impending motion: W sin(angle) = 0.45 × W cos(angle).

tan(angle) = 0.45, so angle = arctan(0.45) = 24.2°.

examples.problem: A 1,000 N crate sits on a level floor with a static friction coefficient of 0.30. A rope pulls on it at 15° above the horizontal. What rope force starts the crate moving?
examples.idea: The upward component of the rope force reduces the normal force, which reduces the friction available. Write equilibrium in both directions at impending motion: horizontal pull = coefficient × (weight minus vertical pull).
examples.steps:
Normal force: N = 1,000 - P sin 15°.

Impending motion: P cos 15° = 0.30(1,000 - P sin 15°).

P = \frac{0.30(1,000)}{cos 15° + 0.30 sin 15°} = \frac{300}{1.044} = 287.5 N.

examples.problem: A 250 N block rests on a 500 N block on a floor, and a cable holds the upper block in place. The coefficient of static friction is 0.35 between the blocks and 0.25 between the lower block and the floor. What horizontal force starts the lower block moving?
examples.idea: Each sliding surface has its own normal force. The top face of the lower block carries the upper block's weight; its bottom face carries both. Friction on both faces opposes the pull.
examples.steps:
Friction on the top face = 0.35 × 250 = 87.5 N.

Friction on the bottom face = 0.25 × (250 + 500) = 187.5 N.

P = 87.5 + 187.5 = 275.0 N.

examples.problem: A 460 N block rests on a plane inclined at 22° to the horizontal. The coefficient of static friction is 0.33. What force, applied parallel to the plane, will start the block moving up the plane?
examples.idea: To start motion up the plane the force must overcome both the component of weight down the plane and the maximum friction, which also acts down the plane when motion is impending upward.
examples.steps:
Weight component down the plane = 460 sin 22° = 172.3 N. Normal force = 460 cos 22° = 426.5 N.

P = 172.3 + 0.33(426.5) = 313.1 N.

examples.problem: A rope passes over a fixed drum with a wrap angle of 180°. The coefficient of friction is 0.23 and the tension on the slack side is 275 N. What is the largest tension the other side can hold before the rope slips?
examples.idea: Friction around a curved surface multiplies tension exponentially: tight-side tension = slack-side tension × e^{(coefficient × wrap angle)}, with the angle in radians.

examples.problem: A 570 N crate is 0.6 m wide and 1.5 m tall, with its weight acting through its centre. A horizontal force is applied at its top edge, and friction is high enough to prevent sliding. What force makes the crate start to tip?
examples.idea: At the point of tipping the floor reaction moves to the edge the crate would rotate about. Take moments about that edge: the push at height h overturns, and the weight at half the width resists.

sections.deep:
Dry friction resists sliding with a force that grows only as large as needed, up to a limit of the static coefficient times the normal force. Below the limit, friction is found from equilibrium, not from the coefficient. At the limit, motion is impending. Once sliding starts, the smaller kinetic coefficient applies.

The normal force is not always the weight: an inclined surface or an angled pull changes it. Some problems must be checked for tipping as well as sliding. Belt friction follows T_{1} = T_{2} e^{coefficient × wrap angle in radians}.
method: Draw the free-body diagram with normal and friction forces; friction opposes impending motion.
Find the normal force from equilibrium perpendicular to the surface.
Compute the maximum friction, coefficient times normal force.
Compare the force needed for equilibrium with that maximum, or set them equal if motion is impending.
On an incline, resolve the weight along and perpendicular to the slope.

sections.primer: Friction is the force that resists sliding between two surfaces. It can grow only up to a limit: the coefficient of friction times the normal force pressing the surfaces together. Below the limit the object stays put; at the limit it is about to slide.
sections.work: Tyre grip on the road is this same friction model; it sets stopping distance and how fast a curve can be taken.
terms: coefficient of friction
the ratio of the largest friction force a surface can supply to the normal force pressing the surfaces together
normal force
the force a surface exerts perpendicular to itself on an object resting or pressing on it
equilibrium
the state of an object that is not accelerating: all forces on it cancel, and so do all their turning effects
symbols: tension on the tight side of the rope
